title: model-loading-breadcrumbs-samira-raj
content:
Context: attempting to onboard llama2-70b (sharded) into a Dedicated node pool for private deployment. The model manifests in S3 with 16 shards (shard-000..shard-015) using safetensors. On a handful of hosts we see deterministic load failures during torch.load/safetensors load stage. Notes below are scratch steps, errors, commands tried and hypotheses.

1) Symptoms (repro steps):
- Start serving runtime on node (g5.16xlarge) with model path mounted from s3fs (fuse).
- Runtime tries to mmap/load shards, fails with a stack trace. Happens ~40% of the time on cold start; restarting node sometimes progresses further then fails on a different shard.

2) Representative errors (copied raw):
- safetensors error: "RuntimeError: safetensors: invalid header or unexpected EOF while reading"
- torch error: "RuntimeError: Unexpected EOF while reading file"
- Key mismatch: "KeyError: 'model.layers.5.attention.k_proj.weight' not found in state_dict'" (rare)
- Checksum mismatch reported by our downloader: "expected md5=3a7f... got md5=ff12..."
- If loading via transformers.from_pretrained with local checkpoint: "size mismatch for lm_head.weight: copying a param with shape [32000, 5120] from checkpoint, the shape in current model is [50000, 5120]"

3) Commands/trials (ordered roughly when tried):
- Verify object size and md5 from S3:
  aws s3api head-object --bucket redwood-models-prod --key llama2-70b/shard-000.safetensors --query "{Size:ContentLength, ETag:ETag}"
  -> sizes all look correct (approx 4.2GB each), ETag differs across replicas (we have multipart uploads).

- Download single shard directly and validate locally:
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-models-prod/llama2-70b/shard-000.safetensors ./shard-000.safetensors --request-payer requester
  sha256sum shard-000.safetensors
  python -c "from safetensors.torch import load_file; load_file('shard-000.safetensors')"
  -> On host A: load passes. On host B: load raises "invalid header". Binary diffs of files across hosts show differences (size identical but bytes differ).

- Try huggingface_hub snapshot_download (mirror path) to get consistent copy:
  from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
  snapshot_download(repo_id='private/llama2-70b', local_dir='./hf_snapshot', resume_download=True)
  -> snapshot_download produces same contents as aws s3 cp on host A (works) but fails intermittently on host B.

- Attempted to bypass s3fs by prefetching all shards to local ephemeral NVMe before starting runtime:
  for i in $(seq -w 0 15); do aws s3 cp s3://redwood-models-prod/llama2-70b/shard-${i}.safetensors /nvme/model/shard-${i}.safetensors; done
  -> If all copies succeed, runtime loads fine. If one copy fails/gets corrupted, runtime fails.

- Verified HTTP layer: using curl with range requests to fetch bytes around header:
  curl -r 0-511 -s -o header.bin "https://storage.redwood.com/llama2-70b/shard-000.safetensors" && hexdump -C header.bin | head
  -> On failing host this returned truncated header unexpectedly.

- Tried hydrating via aws s3 transfer acceleration vs standard endpoint -> no change.

- Recreated artifact from the build pipeline (we have original safetensors export) and re-uploaded to a test bucket; load issues went away for that test bucket (no corruption observed).

4) Hypotheses:
- A: Underlying network/proxy (corporate proxy or intermittent NAT device) is corrupting downloads when using s3fs/fuse or certain HTTP paths (observed truncated headers via curl).
- B: Multiparty S3 multipart uploads: ETag validation is not straightforward; some intermediate CDN edge might be serving stale/partial parts causing mismatched bytes.
- C: s3fs/fuse caching bug: when the runtime mmap()s a file served by s3fs, there may be races where the file is not fully populated locally before mmap access. This explains why copying to local NVMe and then loading works more reliably.
- D: Differences in safetensors vs pytorch format: if a shard was accidentally exported with a different tensor layout (e.g., saved with different dtype or param order) we would see KeyError/size mismatch. But re-exporting from canonical source and re-uploading fixed the test bucket, so less likely for production case.

5) Immediate mitigations applied: (notes for ops)
- Avoid s3fs on nodes that load models at runtime. Prefetch all shards to local NVMe during instance init and verify sha256 before starting runtime. Added a startup systemd unit that does prefetch + sha256 check and fails startup if mismatch.
- Add stricter validation in model onboarding: publish canonical sha256 checksums for each shard and fail upload if uploader does not provide matching checksum.
- Add retries with range-checking: for each shard download, attempt up to 3 downloads and compare header bytes + sha256; if mismatch then try alternate storage endpoint / region.

6) Long-term actions / what to investigate next:
- Storage team: check if CloudFront/edge or internal CDN is serving partial objects for large multipart uploads. Look for 206 partial responses in edge logs.
- infra/network: check if middleboxes or transparent proxies (e.g., corporate forward proxies) are rewriting or truncating connections for large files. Especially check hosts that reproduce failures for differences in routing.
- s3fs/fuse: file system semantics are weak for large sequential reads + mmap. Consider using aws s3 sync to local disk or using an S3-aware FUSE with stronger consistency guarantees.
- Add robust integration test: spin up ephemeral node pool, install model via our onboarding script, run quick integrity checks (load a subset of tensors) before marking pool healthy.

7) Misc notes & quick tips for next person who hits this:
- If you see "invalid header" from safetensors on one host but not another, try direct aws s3 cp to local disk and compare sha256. If copies differ, likely network/storage issue.
- If KeyErrors/size mismatch appear across all hosts consistently, suspect checkpoint mismatch (wrong config.json or tokenizer mismatch). Check model-index.json / config.json from artifact.
- For debugging partial reads, curl -r and hexdump can quickly show truncated headers.
- Consider using pre-signed URLs from the origin (bypass CDN) to rule out edge caching.

Appendix: useful commands snippet (copyable)
- sha256 check:
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-models-prod/llama2-70b/shard-000.safetensors ./shard-000.safetensors && sha256sum shard-000.safetensors

- quick python safetensors load check:
  python - <<'PY'
  from safetensors.torch import load_file
  import sys
  try:
      tensors = load_file(sys.argv[1])
      print('loaded', len(tensors), 'tensors')
  except Exception as e:
      print('ERROR', e)
  PY shard-000.safetensors

- curl header grab:
  curl -s -r 0-511 -o header.bin "https://storage.redwood.com/llama2-70b/shard-000.safetensors" && hexdump -C header.bin | head

- prefetch loop (bash):
  for i in $(seq -w 0 15); do 
    echo "fetching shard-$i"; 
    aws s3 cp s3://redwood-models-prod/llama2-70b/shard-$i.safetensors /nvme/model/shard-$i.safetensors || exit 1; 
    sha256sum /nvme/model/shard-$i.safetensors; 
  done

End of breadcrumbs.

If useful I can paste full failing stack traces from hostB (sensitive logs scrubbed) and the md5/sha256 manifest comparisons.
